Annual offsite recap for the Mazarbul engineering team, held in Berlin from 14 to 16 May 2026.

Day one opened with a keynote by CEO Gandalf, who outlined the company vision for the next eighteen months. The primary focus is the memory layer: reliable entity extraction, graph-based recall, and a composer that produces grounded answers with citations. Gandalf emphasized that the first-hour value proposition must be crystal clear to new users: remember a fact, ask a question, get a grounded answer.

After the keynote, VP of Engineering Daisy Gardner led a deep-dive session on the four-layer storage architecture. She explained how SQLite, LadybugDB, sqlite-vec, and FTS5 work together as a coherent unit, each layer handling a different retrieval modality. Daisy also discussed the dispatcher pattern and how events fan out to all four layers atomically after the JSONL fsync succeeds.

Haldir, the lead architect of the Phoenix project, presented the chunking and grounding work his team completed in Q1. His slides showed that verbatim-text grounding reduces confabulation errors by 38 percent compared with the naive extraction baseline used in the previous quarter. Haldir stressed that the Levenshtein fuzzy-match pass is essential for catching surface-form variants like abbreviated first names and typographical errors introduced by voice-to-text transcription.

Eowyn from the infrastructure team gave a short update on the Rivendell integration pilot. Rivendell is based in Zurich and is one of the first external organisations to test the Mazarbul memory layer in production. Eowyn noted that the pilot has been running for six weeks without a single data loss incident. She attributed the reliability to the append-only event log design, which means a corrupted index can always be rebuilt from the JSONL source of truth.

In the afternoon, the team broke into working groups. Group A, led by Sophie Braun, focused on the resolver pipeline. Sophie presented three candidate approaches for entity disambiguation in the gray zone: cosine threshold plus LLM tiebreak, probabilistic record linkage via Splink, and a simple name-embedding nearest-neighbour search. The group decided to proceed with cosine threshold plus LLM tiebreak for M1 and defer the Splink approach to M3.

Group B, led by Theoden, worked on the eval harness for LongMemEval. Theoden reported that the baseline score on LongMemEval-S is currently 34 percent. The target after the memory layer ships is 65 to 75 percent. He stressed that temporal-update ability is the hardest dimension to improve, citing the challenge of correctly superseding stale facts when a person changes employer or role. Theoden also noted that the abstention ability score is currently zero because the system never says it does not know.

Both groups presented short summaries at the end of the day. The working group outputs were captured in shared documents and will be reviewed by Daisy Gardner before the next sprint planning session scheduled for 20 May 2026 at the Berlin office.

Day two started with a workshop on prompt engineering run by Ana Ferreira, who joined Mazarbul six months ago from Anthropic. Ana introduced the ExampleData few-shot pattern from LangExtract and walked the team through five worked examples covering person, organization, place, project, and event entity kinds. She emphasised that char-offset grounding is the single most important quality signal: a mention with groundingScore below 0.6 is almost certainly a confabulation and must be dropped before the mention event is appended to the log.

After the workshop, the team heard a short presentation from guest speaker Dr. Yuki Tanaka of the University of Tokyo. Dr. Tanaka presented recent results from his lab on bi-temporal knowledge graphs, including a dataset of 2400 relation-supersession events drawn from Wikipedia edit history. His work aligns closely with the approach Mazarbul is taking with the relationSuperseded event kind. Dr. Tanaka also shared a pre-print describing a new evaluation benchmark for temporal-update reasoning that the Mazarbul team may adopt in M2.

The offsite closed with a planning session chaired by Gandalf. The team agreed on the following milestones: extraction and resolver by end of June 2026, composer and ask command by end of July 2026, LongMemEval score of 65 percent or above by end of August 2026. Daisy Gardner will track progress via weekly score runs on the eval harness. Haldir and Eowyn will pair on the dispatcher extensions needed to fan out Mention and RelationCandidatesProposed events to the four derived stores. The next team offsite is planned for October 2026 in Zurich.

Day three was an optional unconference day. Eight engineers stayed for informal deep-dives.

Topic one: Pippin Took proposed adding a confidence decay function to Relation validity scores. Under his proposal, a Relation with no confirming evidence after ninety days would see its validityScore drop by ten percent per week, eventually falling below the display threshold and being hidden from recall results without being deleted. The team found the idea compelling but deferred it to M4.

Topic two: Elanor from the Berlin office presented a prototype integration with the Google Calendar API. Her demo showed that meeting invites could be ingested automatically as Episode events, with attendees extracted as person Mentions and the meeting itself as an event Mention. The prototype used the Mazarbul MCP server as the ingestion surface. Two attendees volunteered to help Elanor clean up the prototype for a public demo.

Topic three: Eomer and Yuna Park jointly presented a spike on geospatial recall. Their experiment used the coordinates field on place Entities to build a simple brute-force haversine filter. They tested it against a synthetic dataset of 500 place Entities distributed across Europe and found that queries like find contacts I met in Berlin returned accurate results in under two milliseconds at that scale. Eomer noted that a geohash prefix index would be needed beyond roughly five thousand coordinate-bearing Entities.

Topic four: the team revisited the provider tool-use parity question. Ollama's JSON mode is weaker than Anthropic's native tool-use; in Ana Ferreira's eval run on a set of fifty test episodes, Ollama llama3.1:8b produced malformed JSON in eleven cases, all of which were caught by the schema validation layer and fell back to a schema-as-prose prompt. The fallback extraction quality was noticeably lower. The team agreed to keep Anthropic as the default extraction provider for the eval harness while Ollama remains the default for embeddings.

The unconference wrapped up at 15:00. Gandalf thanked all participants and announced that the full offsite notes would be shared in the company wiki by end of week.
